title: Be a Sales Superstar: 21 Great Ways to Sell More, Faster, Easier in Tough Markets
author: Brian Tracy
summary:
Be a Sales Superstar is Brian Tracy's compact, tactics-focused sales book, organized as twenty-one short, largely self-contained chapters, each built around a single actionable sales principle rather than a single overarching narrative argument. The book's premise, stated early and returned to throughout, is that selling success is not a matter of talent or charisma but of consistently applying a specific, learnable set of behaviors, especially around prospecting discipline, preparation, and follow-through, in markets that are difficult or highly competitive.

Tracy structures the book around what he frames as the highest-leverage activities in selling: identifying and focusing on the right prospects rather than spreading effort evenly across all potential customers, preparing thoroughly before every sales call rather than relying on improvisation, and building genuine trust and rapport as a prerequisite for any sale rather than treating persuasion techniques as a substitute for a real relationship. Across many of the twenty-one chapters, he returns to the idea that customers buy from salespeople they trust and perceive as credible experts, and that most sales are lost not through a failure of closing technique but through a failure to establish that trust early in the process.

A second major thread concerns objection handling and closing, where Tracy argues that most objections are predictable and can be anticipated and prepared for in advance, turning what feels to inexperienced salespeople like an unpredictable confrontation into a scripted, rehearsable part of the process. He is emphatic that a sale is not complete until a specific action — a signature, a payment, a commitment — has occurred, and devotes several chapters to specific closing techniques and the psychological reluctance many salespeople feel about asking directly for the sale.

The book closes on the theme of self-management: time allocation, goal-setting, and the compounding effect of daily disciplined activity (a fixed number of prospecting calls, a fixed amount of preparation time) over inconsistent bursts of effort. Tracy's overall throughline, restated in different forms across the twenty-one chapters, is that sales performance is a numbers-driven, disciplined craft that rewards consistent application of known techniques far more than it rewards natural talent or occasional inspired effort.

sections.title: Commit to Excellence
sections.summary:
This opening chapter argues that the starting point for sales success is a personal decision to commit to becoming excellent at the craft, rather than treating selling as a temporary or lesser activity. Tracy frames this commitment as the foundation on which all subsequent technique-based chapters depend.

He argues that top-performing salespeople distinguish themselves less by innate talent than by a deliberate, ongoing commitment to self-improvement, continuous learning, and treating selling as a respected profession rather than a fallback career. The chapter sets an expectation that the rest of the book's tactics will only work for readers who have made this underlying commitment.

It closes by previewing the book's practical structure, framing the following twenty chapters as specific expressions of this initial commitment to excellence.
keyLessons: Sustained sales excellence begins with a deliberate personal decision to commit to the craft, not just a wish to improve.
Treating selling as a respected profession, worthy of ongoing study, changes how consistently a person practices its component skills.
Natural talent matters less than consistent, deliberate effort over time in determining top sales performance.

sections.title: Know Your Product and Your Customer
sections.summary:
This chapter argues that deep product knowledge and customer research are prerequisites for credibility, not optional extras, and that under-prepared salespeople lose trust quickly regardless of their interpersonal skill. It sets thorough preparation as a recurring value throughout the book.

Tracy recommends specific research habits before any sales call, including understanding a prospect's business, competitors, and likely priorities, arguing that this preparation shortens the sales cycle by letting the salesperson speak directly to the prospect's actual situation rather than a generic pitch.

The chapter closes by linking preparation to the trust-building theme developed further in later chapters, arguing that visible preparation is itself one of the fastest ways to establish credibility with a new prospect.
keyLessons: Deep product knowledge lets a salesperson answer questions confidently, which builds credibility faster than charisma alone.
Researching a specific prospect's business and priorities before a call allows a more targeted, relevant pitch.
Visible preparation is itself a trust-building signal to a new prospect, independent of the pitch's content.

sections.title: Position Yourself as the Expert
sections.summary:
This chapter develops the idea that prospects buy more readily from salespeople they perceive as knowledgeable, credible experts in their field, rather than from generic order-takers. It introduces specific tactics for establishing this expert positioning early in a sales relationship.

Tracy recommends leading with diagnostic questions and useful, unbiased information rather than an immediate pitch, arguing that prospects extend more trust to someone who appears focused on solving their problem than to someone who appears focused only on making a sale.

The chapter closes by connecting expert positioning to reduced price sensitivity, arguing that prospects who trust a salesperson's expertise are less likely to shop primarily on price.
keyLessons: Leading with diagnostic questions rather than an immediate pitch signals genuine problem-solving intent.
Perceived expertise reduces a prospect's price sensitivity, since trust substitutes for exhaustive comparison shopping.
Expert positioning is built through early behavior in the relationship, not asserted through claims alone.

sections.title: Prospect Continuously
sections.summary:
This chapter argues that consistent, disciplined prospecting is the single highest-leverage activity in sales, and that inconsistent income or performance is most often traceable to inconsistent prospecting activity rather than to weak closing skill. It frames prospecting as a scheduled, non-negotiable daily habit rather than an occasional task.

Tracy recommends specific daily quotas for prospecting activity and warns against the common trap of prospecting heavily when the pipeline feels empty and stopping once it fills, which produces a boom-and-bust income cycle. He connects this to the book's broader theme of disciplined, repeated activity outperforming inconsistent bursts of effort.

The chapter closes by setting up the following chapters' focus on qualifying and focusing prospecting effort on the right targets, rather than pursuing volume indiscriminately.
keyLessons: Inconsistent sales results usually trace back to inconsistent prospecting activity, not weak closing technique.
Scheduling prospecting as a fixed daily habit avoids the boom-and-bust cycle of prospecting only when the pipeline is empty.
Prospecting discipline compounds over time, similarly to other high-leverage habits described later in the book.

sections.title: Qualify Prospects Thoroughly
sections.summary:
This chapter shifts from prospecting volume to prospecting quality, arguing that time spent pursuing poorly qualified prospects is one of the most common and costly inefficiencies in sales. It introduces specific criteria for assessing whether a prospect has genuine need, budget, and authority to buy.

Tracy provides a framework of qualifying questions designed to surface these factors early, arguing that disqualifying a poor-fit prospect quickly, though uncomfortable, frees up time for better-fit opportunities and ultimately raises overall close rates.

The chapter closes by linking qualification discipline to the objection-handling and closing chapters later in the book, noting that well-qualified prospects generate fewer late-stage objections because their fit was established early.
keyLessons: Time spent on poorly qualified prospects is one of the most common inefficiencies in a sales process.
Assessing need, budget, and authority early avoids investing effort in deals that were never likely to close.
Well-qualified prospects tend to raise fewer serious objections later in the process, since fit issues surface earlier.

sections.title: Handle Objections with Confidence
sections.summary:
This chapter reframes objections as a normal, predictable, and even useful part of the sales process rather than a sign of failure, arguing that most objections a salesperson will encounter fall into a small, anticipatable set. It provides a general method for responding to objections calmly rather than defensively.

Tracy recommends preparing responses to the most common objections in advance, treating this preparation as a rehearsable skill rather than an improvised confrontation, and emphasizes acknowledging an objection's legitimacy before responding to it, rather than dismissing it.

The chapter closes by connecting confident objection handling to the closing chapters that follow, arguing that unresolved objections, more than any other single factor, are what prevent salespeople from asking directly for the close.
keyLessons: Most sales objections fall into a small, predictable set that can be anticipated and prepared for in advance.
Acknowledging an objection's legitimacy before responding reduces defensiveness on both sides of the conversation.
Objections are a normal part of the process, not evidence that a sale has failed.

sections.title: Close the Sale
sections.summary:
This chapter addresses the psychological reluctance many salespeople feel about directly asking for a commitment, arguing that a sale is not complete until a specific action has occurred, and that many otherwise well-run sales processes fail simply because no one asked clearly for the close. It introduces several specific closing techniques and when to use each.

Tracy stresses reading buying signals throughout a conversation rather than waiting for an artificial "closing moment," and argues that asking for the sale directly, though uncomfortable for many salespeople, is far less risky than the lost sales caused by never asking clearly at all.

The chapter closes the book's technical, tactic-by-tactic core by transitioning into the closing chapters on self-management, framing consistent closing performance as dependent on the discipline established throughout the rest of the book.
keyLessons: A sale is not complete until a specific commitment action has occurred; enthusiasm alone is not a sale.
Reading buying signals throughout the conversation, not just at a designated "closing moment," identifies more opportunities to ask for commitment.
Reluctance to ask directly for the sale is a common, addressable psychological barrier, not a fixed trait.

sections.title: Manage Yourself for Peak Performance
sections.summary:
The closing chapter shifts to time management, goal-setting, and daily discipline, arguing that consistent application of the book's techniques, sustained over time, is what separates top performers from average ones — not any single technique in isolation. It ties the book's individual tactics back to the opening chapter's theme of personal commitment.

Tracy recommends specific daily and weekly planning habits, protecting prime selling hours from administrative distraction, and setting concrete, measurable goals rather than vague aspirations. He frames self-discipline as the compounding multiplier that determines whether the rest of the book's techniques actually get applied consistently enough to matter.

The book closes by restating its throughline: that sales excellence is a learnable, disciplined craft, achievable by anyone willing to apply its principles consistently rather than sporadically.
keyLessons: Protecting prime selling hours from administrative and low-value tasks materially increases effective selling time.
Concrete, measurable goals produce more consistent action than vague aspirations to "sell more."
Consistent application of known techniques over time, not any single tactic, is what ultimately separates top performers from average ones.
Treat selling as a craft worth deliberate, ongoing study, not a talent you either have or lack.
Prepare thoroughly on both product knowledge and a specific prospect's situation before every sales call.
Lead with diagnostic questions and useful information to build expert positioning before pitching.
Schedule prospecting as a fixed daily habit to avoid boom-and-bust income cycles.
Qualify prospects on need, budget, and authority early, and disqualify poor fits quickly rather than chasing volume.
Prepare responses to common objections in advance and acknowledge their legitimacy before responding.
Ask directly and clearly for the sale; enthusiasm and rapport alone do not constitute a completed sale.
Protect prime selling hours from low-value tasks and set concrete, measurable goals to sustain consistent activity.

conceptsFrameworks.name: Expert Positioning
conceptsFrameworks.definition: The practice of establishing credibility with a prospect by leading with diagnostic questions and useful, unbiased information rather than an immediate sales pitch, on the premise that prospects extend more trust — and are less price-sensitive — toward salespeople they perceive as knowledgeable experts rather than as order-takers.

conceptsFrameworks.name: Prospecting Discipline
conceptsFrameworks.definition: Tracy's framework for treating prospecting as a fixed, scheduled daily activity with a consistent quota, rather than an occasional task performed only when the sales pipeline feels empty, on the premise that inconsistent prospecting is the primary cause of inconsistent sales income.

conceptsFrameworks.name: Qualification Criteria (Need, Budget, Authority)
conceptsFrameworks.definition: A framework for assessing early in a sales conversation whether a prospect has genuine need for the product, sufficient budget, and the authority to make or influence the purchase decision, used to decide quickly whether to invest further time in a given prospect.

actionSteps: Before your next five prospect calls, spend fifteen minutes researching the specific prospect's business and likely priorities, and open the call with a diagnostic question rather than a pitch.
Set a fixed daily or weekly prospecting quota (a specific number of new contacts) and track it for two weeks regardless of how full your current pipeline feels.
Write out your three most common sales objections and draft a calm, non-defensive response to each that acknowledges the objection's legitimacy before addressing it.
In your next qualified sales conversation, practice directly asking for the specific next action (signature, payment, meeting) rather than waiting for the prospect to bring it up.
reflectionQuestions: Where in your current sales process do you tend to avoid asking directly for a commitment, and what does that avoidance seem to be protecting you from?
Looking at your last ten prospects, how many would have passed a genuine need/budget/authority check before you invested significant time in them?

points: The book's twenty-one-chapter, tactic-by-tactic structure trades depth for breadth; several techniques are described briefly enough that readers may need Tracy's longer works (like The Psychology of Selling) for fuller treatment of the underlying psychology.

The advice is largely generic across product types and sales contexts (B2B, B2C, high-ticket, transactional), so some techniques will need real adaptation for a reader's specific industry rather than being applied exactly as written.

As with much of Tracy's sales writing, claims about "what top performers do" rest primarily on his own decades of sales training experience and anecdote rather than on cited, controlled research comparing techniques.

The book's tactics assume a reasonably conventional outbound or relationship-based sales environment; readers in heavily inbound, self-serve, or digitally mediated sales motions may find some prospecting advice less directly applicable without adaptation.
criticalTake.contextNote: Brian Tracy's core sales framework here has remained popular and widely referenced in sales training for years, though the specific prospecting tactics described predate the more recent shift toward digital and social-selling channels, which some sales organizations now treat as a significant complement to the more traditional call-and-visit prospecting emphasized in the book.

whoThisIsFor: Salespeople and small business owners who want a fast, tactic-by-tactic refresher on core sales fundamentals rather than a single deep theoretical framework.
whenToReadThis: Useful as a pre-call or weekly refresher, given its short, modular chapter structure, rather than as a single cover-to-cover deep study.

authorBio.name: Brian Tracy
authorBio.bio:
Brian Tracy (born 1944) is a Canadian-American author, motivational speaker, and sales trainer who built his career after early jobs in sales and business development, later founding Brian Tracy International to deliver sales and leadership training globally. He is one of the most prolific and widely translated authors in the sales and personal development genre, having written dozens of books over several decades.

Tracy's work is generally characterized by an emphasis on practical, immediately applicable technique over abstract theory, often distilled into short, numbered lists of principles, a format reflected in this book's twenty-one-chapter structure. His seminars and corporate training programs have been delivered to a wide range of companies and sales organizations internationally.

He continues to write, speak, and produce training content across sales, leadership, and personal achievement topics.

sourceNotes:
Synthesis is based on general knowledge of Brian Tracy's well-documented sales-training framework and this book's structure; several quotes are commonly and consistently attributed to Tracy across his sales writing but could not be verified as exact, page-specific wording for this particular title, which is flagged directly in the relevant quote entries rather than presented as fully confirmed.
